facts.quote: It follows Breuer's demonstration "House in the Museum Garden" built the year before for the Museum of Modern Art, which now sits at the Rockefeller Kykuit estate in New York's Hudson Valley.

facts.fact: Breuer did three commissions on the site in 1950–1953 (a main house, a studio and a pool and porch), with an 18 x 10 ft pool mural wall by Alexander Calder.
facts.quote: The site boasts three separate architectural commissions by Breuer between 1950–1953: a main house, a studio, and pool and porch redesign, with the latter featuring an 18'x10' pool mural wall by friend and sculptor, Alexander Calder.

facts.fact: The Bauhaus artist Xanti Schawinsky painted an interior mural wall at the same time.
facts.quote: During this time, fellow first-generation Bauhaus friend and artist, Xanti Schawinsky, executed an interior mural wall as well.

facts.fact: With John Johansen's neighbouring Huvelle House (1953), it was one of the first two modern homes in Litchfield.
facts.quote: The Stillman House sits adjacent the Huvelle House (1953) by John M. Johansen and together, they represent the first and second modern homes in Litchfield, existing between a forest reserve and the town's historic North Street.

facts.fact: In reaction to these houses, the Borough of Litchfield restricts modern design within its historic boundaries.
facts.quote: To date, and in reaction to these homes, the Borough of Litchfield restricts the further use of modern design within its borough's historic boundaries as protection to its Colonial and Greek Revival heritage.

facts.fact: Both houses were restored in the 2010s and won a Docomomo US Citation of Merit in 2014.
facts.quote: Both Stillman House I and the Huvelle House were restored in the 2010s, garnering a 2014 Citations of Merit from Docomomo US, with the jury noting "in addition to repairing structural damage, the owners removed later additions to the Stillman House and returned a removed floating porch and staircase to a Breuer-designed swimming pool.

facts.fact: The house in Madison is a Prairie School home by Louis Sullivan and George Grant Elmslie, one of only a few Sullivan houses, and a National Historic Landmark.
facts.quote: Designed by Louis H. Sullivan and George Grant Elmslie, it is one of just a few residential designs by Sullivan, and one of only two Sullivan designs in Wisconsin. It is designated a National Historic Landmark.

facts.fact: Richard T. Crane had it built as a present for his granddaughter Josephine and her husband, the biochemistry professor Harold C. Bradley.
facts.quote: When Harold C. Bradley, a biochemistry professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a founder of the Hoofers Club, married Josephine Crane, her grandfather Richard T. Crane built this house for them as a present.

facts.fact: The two-storey house has a T-shaped plan with cantilevered sections holding sleeping porches, and a porte-cochère at the back.
facts.quote: The house is two stories with a T-shaped footprint, with distinctive cantilevered sections that hold sleeping porches. (A sleeping porch was a way to deal with hot summer nights before there was air conditioning.) At the back is a porte-cochère.

facts.fact: The architects also designed the furniture, rugs, draperies and fixtures.
facts.quote: The architects also designed furniture, rugs, draperies and fixtures inside.

facts.fact: Elmslie sketched all the drawings, with only occasional suggestions from Sullivan.
facts.quote: The Bradley House was "designed by Elmslie with only occasional suggestions from Sullivan." All drawings of the building were sketched by Elmslie and many of the architectural details are consistent with the style he would develop later in his career with William Gray Purcell.

facts.fact: It was the last building Elmslie designed with Sullivan before leaving in 1909 to partner with Purcell.
facts.quote: The Bradley House was the last building Elmslie designed while with Sullivan; he left to partner with Purcell in 1909.

facts.fact: The Bradleys rejected an earlier, larger cruciform design, and Elmslie reworked it on a smaller scale with two cantilevered sleeping porches.
facts.quote: However, the Bradleys rejected this draft as too large. Elmslie reenvisioned the house on a smaller scale and included a pair of cantilevered sleeping porches on the second floor.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973 and named a National Historic Landmark in 1976.
facts.quote: The Harold C. Bradley House was entered in the National Register of Historic Places in 1973 and declared a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

facts.fact: The organist Erich Piasetzki became choir director and organist at the Offenbarungskirche in Friedrichshain, Berlin, after 1958.
facts.quote: After 1958 he became choral director and organist at the Offenbarungskirche, in Friedrichshain, Berlin.

facts.fact: The Sainte-Thérèse-de-l'Enfant-Jésus church by Roger-Henri Expert is one of the works of modern architecture in Metz; the article dates it 1934.
facts.quote: Modern architecture can also be seen in the town with works of French architects Roger-Henri Expert (Sainte-Thérèse-de-l'Enfant-Jésus church, 1934), Georges-Henri Pingusson (Fire Station, 1960) and Jean Dubuisson (subdivisions, 1960s).

facts.fact: Naturtheater Grötzingen is an open-air woodland theatre in Grötzingen, Baden-Württemberg.
facts.quote: Naturtheater Grötzingen  is a sylvan theatre in Grötzingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany.

facts.fact: It is a thin concrete shell, dated 1954 in the article, seating 850 people.
facts.quote: It is a thin concrete shell built in 1954 and seats an audience of 850.

facts.fact: It was designed by the architect Michael Balz and the structural engineer Heinz Isler.
facts.quote: It was designed by architect Michael Balz and structural engineer Heinz Isler.

facts.fact: La Spezia Cathedral, the Cathedral of Christ the King, was built between 1956 and 1975 to designs by Adalberto Libera.
facts.quote: It is the cathedral of the Diocese of La Spezia-Sarzana-Brugnato. It was built between 1956 and 1975, according to designs by Adalberto Libera.

facts.fact: An earlier competition was won by Brenno Del Giudice, but works were postponed for over 25 years and his design was never built.
facts.quote: A competition was announced, in which the winning entry was that of the architect Brenno Del Giudice, Still, the works were postponed by more than 25 years until the mid-1950s and Del Giudice's designs were never implemented.

facts.fact: Libera, a Rationalist architect chosen in 1956, used the raised site on Piazza Europa to stress the building's monumentality.
facts.quote: In the revived project of 1956, the Rationalist architect Adalberto Libera was chosen, who availed himself of the potential of the elevated site on the vast Piazza Europa to emphasise the monumentality of the religious building.

facts.fact: When Libera died in 1963 the building was unfinished; the local architect Cesare Galeazzi completed it with some changes of his own, and it was consecrated in 1975.
facts.quote: On the death of Libera in 1963, the building was still unfinished, and its completion was entrusted to the local architect Cesare Galeazzi, who resumed construction, incorporating some variations of his own. In 1975, the works were completed, and the cathedral was consecrated and dedicated to Christ King of the Ages (Cristo Re dei Secoli).

facts.fact: The building has a circular plan and an outer wall shaped as a hyperboloid of one sheet, with no openings.
facts.quote: The exterior of the imposing structure is strongly characterised by its circular plan and the external wall, in the shape of a hyperboloid of one sheet, without any openings.

facts.fact: Light enters through the centre of a 50-metre dome carried on 12 massive columns that symbolise the Apostles.
facts.quote: The interior receives light from the opening in the centre of the vast cupola, with a diameter of 50 metres, supported by 12 massive columns symbolising the Apostles.

facts.fact: A band of stained glass runs around the perimeter of the main space as a second source of light.
facts.quote: A second source of light comes from a band of stained glass windows running around the perimeter of the main space.

facts.fact: The gently sloping white and grey marble floor converges on the central white marble altar.
facts.quote: The pavement of white and grey marble, slightly sloping, converges towards the central altar of white marble, while the presbytery, paved in red marble, is slightly raised.

facts.fact: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum was set up in August 1955 together with the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Hall, now the International Conference Center Hiroshima.
facts.quote: The museum was established in August 1955 with the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Hall (now the International Conference Center Hiroshima).

facts.fact: Kenneth Macpherson and Bryher commissioned the house at La Tour-de-Peilz from the art director and architect Alexander Ferenczy and moved in in September 1931.
facts.quote: In September 1931, Macpherson and Bryher moved to a new home at La Tour-de-Peilz, which they had commissioned art director and architect Alexander Ferenczy to build.

facts.fact: After Ferenczy died, Hermann Henselmann, then his employee, completed the work.
facts.quote: Following Ferenczy's death, the work was completed by Hermann Henselmann, then an employee of Ferenczy's, who subsequently went on to claim ownership of the entire project .

facts.fact: Henselmann's works list dates the villa 1929–1931, with Alexander Ferenczy.
facts.quote: 1929-1931: Villa Kenwin, La Tour-de-Peilz, Chemin du Vallon 19, 1820 Montreux; (Switzerland), with Alexander Ferenczy

facts.fact: The house overlooks Lake Geneva; its name joins Kenneth and Winifred, and it was designed as both a home and a film studio, though there is no evidence it was used as a studio.
facts.quote: The home, which overlooked Lake Geneva, came to be known as Kenwin, derived from the names, Kenneth and Winifred, and was designed as both a film studio (although there is no evidence it was used as such) and home.

facts.fact: During the war, Bryher used Kenwin as a staging post for refugees escaping Nazi Germany.
facts.quote: (During the war years, Bryher used Kenwin as a staging post for the evacuation of refugees from Nazi Germany.)

facts.fact: The WRVA Building is an 18,000 sq ft building in Richmond's historic Church Hill district.
facts.quote: The WRVA Building is an 18,000-square-foot (1,700 m2) building located at 200 N. 22nd St. in the historic Church Hill district of Richmond, Virginia.

facts.fact: Philip Johnson designed it, while at the firm Budina and Freeman, to house WRVA, one of Virginia's first radio stations.
facts.quote: Designed by world-renowned architect Philip Johnson while he was at the architectural firm of Budina and Freeman, it was originally built to house WRVA (AM), one of Virginia's first broadcast radio stations.

facts.fact: It is considered one of Richmond's most visible and important mid-20th-century landmarks.
facts.quote: The building is considered "one of the city's most visible and important mid-20th-century architectural landmarks."

facts.fact: In 2007–2008 it had a $5.4 million renovation for the child services charity ChildSavers.
facts.quote: From 2007 until 2008, the WRVA Building underwent an extensive $5.4 million renovation for use by ChildSavers.

facts.fact: The Richmond firm Baskervill designed the adaptive reuse with few structural changes.
facts.quote: Baskervill, a Richmond architecture firm, designed its adaptive reuse, making few structural changes.

facts.fact: The school stands on Frankford Avenue in Holmesburg, Northeast Philadelphia, and is part of the School District of Philadelphia.
facts.quote: Joseph H. Brown Elementary School is an elementary school on Frankford Avenue at Stanwood Street in Holmesburg, in the Northeast Philadelphia area of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, currently serving students from kindergarten to eighth grade. It is part of the School District of Philadelphia.

facts.fact: The building was built in 1937, replacing an earlier school on the same site.
facts.quote: The current school building was constructed in 1937, replacing an earlier building on the same site.

facts.fact: It was designed by Irwin T. Catharine, then the school district's main architect, and is an example of Art Deco and Moderne architecture.
facts.quote: The school building was designed by Irwin T. Catharine, then the Philadelphia School District's main architect, and is an exemplar of the Art Deco and Moderne schools of architecture.

facts.fact: Catharine was chief architect of Philadelphia's public schools from 1920 to 1937; his buildings ran from Gothic Revival to Streamline Moderne, and this school was his last project.
facts.quote: Irwin Thornton Catharine (October 22, 1883 – March 3, 1944) was the chief architect of Philadelphia public schools from 1920 until his retirement in 1937.  Buildings built during Catharine's tenure ranged from Gothic Revival, as in the case of Simon Gratz High School, to Streamline Moderne, as in his last project, Joseph H. Brown Elementary School.

facts.fact: The school is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: Joseph H. Brown School, 8118-8120 Frankford Ave., NRHP-listed

facts.fact: The Schönberg Tower, at 793 m above sea level south-west of Pfullingen, is a highly visible landmark, nicknamed 'Pfullinger underpants', and was completed in 1906.
facts.quote: The Schönberg Tower (793 m above sea level. NN), popularly known as "Pfullenger Onderhos" (Pfullinger underpants), in the southwest of the town, forms highly visible landmark of the city and was completed 1906.

facts.fact: The Baird House in Amherst is the only Frank Lloyd Wright design in Massachusetts.
facts.quote: It is the only Wright design in Massachusetts.

facts.fact: The Usonian house was planned and built in 1940 for the Amherst College English professor Theodore Baird.
facts.quote: The Usonian house was planned and built in 1940 for Amherst College English professor Theodore Baird.

facts.fact: With no local contractor able to do the work, Wright's protégé William Wesley Peters built it.
facts.quote: They were unable to locate contractors in the area who were able to do the work, so the construction work was done by Wright protégé William Wesley Peters.

facts.fact: It was the only Usonian house whose materials were prefabricated, partly in a New Jersey factory, before reaching the site.
facts.quote: Part of the construction work was done at a factory in New Jersey, and moved to Amherst for final assembly.  The house was the only Usonian for which the materials were prefabricated before being brought to the site.

facts.fact: It has brick, cypress wood and glass façades and a flat roof cantilevered far over a carport.
facts.quote: It is a single-family house with brick, cypress wood and glass façades and a flat roof highly cantilevered over a carport.

facts.fact: It is heated by hot-water pipes in the concrete floor.
facts.quote: Heating is conveyed by pipes distributing hot water through the concrete floor.

facts.fact: The property was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.
facts.quote: The property, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985, also includes a 4-acre (1.6 ha) woodlot that extends behind the house and neighboring properties on Shays Street.

facts.fact: The Defence Corps Building in central Jyväskylä was designed by Alvar Aalto and completed in 1929.
facts.quote: The Defence Corps Building (Finnish: Suojeluskuntatalo), also known as the Government Building (Finnish: Valtiontalo), is a public building located in central Jyväskylä, Finland, designed by the Finnish architect Alvar Aalto, and completed in 1929.

facts.fact: Aalto's entry 'Intra Muros' came only second in the 1925 competition, but the committee chose it as the basis for the building.
facts.quote: Although Aalto's design Intra Muros only finished second, the commissioning committee nevertheless chose it as the basis for their new building.

facts.fact: It is one of Aalto's early major designs, made when he was 28, and marks a move from Nordic Classicism towards Functionalism.
facts.quote: The building is notable as one of Aalto's earlier major designs from when he was aged only 28 and still making his name. Stylistically, it reflects a transition away from the Nordic Classicism still popular in the 1920s, and towards the more modern Functionalism which came to dominate much of the 1930s and early 1940s.

facts.fact: It is one of the most important surviving examples of late Nordic Classicism.
facts.quote: It is one of the most important surviving examples of late Nordic Classicism.

facts.fact: The interior uses Poul Henningsen's three-shade lamps and Villeroy & Boch Mettlach floor tiles, then rare in Finland.
facts.quote: The interior light fittings comprise the Danish Poul Henningsen's contemporary, now iconic three-shade designs. The flooring materials include the Mettlach tiles of Villeroy & Boch, a rarity in Finland at the time.

facts.fact: It was designed as a mixed-use complex with a cinema, restaurants, shops, a bank, sports spaces and the Defence Corps' assembly hall.
facts.quote: Originally the building was designed as a mixed-use, multi-tenant complex, housing a cinema, restaurants, retail and banking facilities, sporting venues, as well as the assembly hall and other functions of the Defence Corps.

facts.fact: The Finnish state took it over in 1934, and it has mostly been called Valtiontalo (State House) since.
facts.quote: However, the Defence Corps only possessed the building for five years, and in 1934 it was acquired by the Finnish state, and has since then most commonly been referred to as Valtiontalo (lit. 'State House', or 'Government Building').

facts.fact: After years of decay it was comprehensively renovated and extended from 2017, finishing in late 2020.
facts.quote: Starting in 2017, the building was comprehensively renovated, as well as extended with attached new-build properties. The renovation was completed in late 2020.

facts.fact: The Kunstgebäude on Stuttgart's Schloßplatz was designed by Theodor Fischer and has housed the Württembergischer Kunstverein since 1913.
facts.quote: The Württembergischer Kunstverein has been based in the art building on Schloßplatz designed by Theodor Fischer since 1913 and has seen itself as a place for dealing with contemporary art ever since.

facts.fact: The Kunstverein, founded in 1827, is one of the oldest art associations in Germany.
facts.quote: The Württembergischer Kunstverein Stuttgart was founded in 1827 and is one of the oldest art associations in Germany.

facts.fact: The building was almost completely destroyed in the Second World War; its rebuilding, with a modern extension, was finished in 1961.
facts.quote: The art building was almost completely destroyed during the Second World War. The reconstruction, which is linked to a modern extension building, was only completed in 1961.

facts.fact: Today it combines the historic domed hall and galleries, a new square hall by Paul Bonatz and Günther Wilhelm, and a glass wing linking old and new.
facts.quote: The gallery of the city of Stuttgart also moved into the rooms of the art building with the Kunstverein, which now consists of the historic complex with a domed hall and gallery rooms, the new so-called quadrangular hall designed by Paul Bonatz and Günther Wilhelm, and a glass connecting wing between the old and new buildings.

facts.fact: In March 1933 the Nazis closed the first major Oskar Schlemmer retrospective here before it opened.
facts.quote: In March 1933, for example, the first major retrospective of Oskar Schlemmer, with his main work Bauhaus Stairs, was closed by the new rulers before it even opened.

facts.fact: The Marion Palace Theatre is a movie palace built in 1928 for the Young Amusement Company, at a cost of $500,000.
facts.quote: The Marion Palace Theatre is a movie palace constructed in 1928 in Marion, Ohio, United States for the Young Amusement Company. The original cost of the project was $500,000 ($7.5 million in 2021 dollars).

facts.fact: It is on the National Register of Historic Places for its importance to the atmospheric theatre style of the 1920s.
facts.quote: It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places because of its significance to the atmospheric theatre architectural style popular in the United States during the 1920s.

facts.fact: John Eberson designed it as an atmospheric theatre to the owner V.U. Young's brief for 'A Spanish Castle' or 'A Palace in Old Spain'.
facts.quote: The Marion Palace was designed by John Eberson as an atmospheric theatre. Eberson designed it to fit the vision of owner V.U. Young for "A Spanish Castle" or "A Palace in Old Spain."

facts.fact: Its style is best described as Spanish Colonial Revival.
facts.quote: The theatre is best described as designed in the Spanish Colonial Revival architecture style.

facts.fact: Inside, patrons pass from the lobby through an arcade into a courtyard on a hill, and the balcony is ringed by a Spanish town wall.
facts.quote: Inside, Eberson transitions the patrons from a lobby through wooden doors to an arcade (at the rear of the orchestra) and into a courtyard on a hill. From the balcony, patrons are surrounded by a Spanish town wall and have the same view a resident would have from a high building looking down on the courtyard.

facts.fact: Stars twinkle through holes in the blue plaster ceiling, and a hidden projector casts moving clouds across it.
facts.quote: Stars are designed in constellation patterns in the ceiling and twinkle through holes in the plaster during performances. A Brenkert Brenograph Jr. projector, hidden in the east side wall, projects clouds on the ceiling, further creating an outdoor illusion.

facts.fact: It was one of the last atmospheric theatres built in the United States, opening on 30 August 1928.
facts.quote: The theatre opened on August 30, 1928, becoming the company's tenth theatre. A movie palace, it was one of the last to be built in the atmospheric theatre style in the United States.

facts.fact: It was fully restored in 1975–1976 by the Palace Cultural Arts Association, with Eberson's son Drew helping to guide the work.
facts.quote: The theatre building was completely restored in 1975–1976 after ownership was transferred to a local nonprofit group, the Palace Cultural Arts Association, under the leadership of John Keggan and his Palace Guard. John Eberson's son, Drew Eberson, helped guide the restoration.

facts.fact: Designed by James Brown Lord in the Italian Renaissance style, the library has a three-storey limestone facade.
facts.quote: Designed by James Brown Lord in the Italian Renaissance style, the building has a three-story-high limestone facade.

facts.fact: Paid for by Andrew Carnegie, it opened in December 1902 as the first Carnegie library in Manhattan.
facts.quote: Built with funds from Andrew Carnegie, it opened in December 1902 as the first Carnegie library in Manhattan.

facts.fact: Like many Manhattan Carnegie libraries it sits mid-block, and it measures 40 by 90 feet.
facts.quote: It is an Italian Renaissance-style Carnegie library designed by James Brown Lord, and, like many of Manhattan's Carnegie libraries, is located in the middle of a block. The building measures 40 by 90 feet (12 by 27 m) across.

facts.fact: The Landmarks Preservation Commission called it one of New York's most elegant adaptations of the Palladian style to a modern public building.
facts.quote: The New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC) has described the building as "one of New York's most elegant adaptions of the Palladian style to a modern public building".

facts.fact: It was one of Lord's last designs built before his death, and cost $70,000.
facts.quote: It was one of Lord's final designs to be built before his death. The building had cost $70,000 to build (equivalent to $2,605,000 in 2025).

facts.fact: The third floor first held a German-language collection for Yorkville's large German population.
facts.quote: Originally, the building had a German-language collection on the third floor to cater to Yorkville's large German population.

facts.fact: It was renovated in 1960 and the late 1980s, and is a New York City landmark listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
facts.quote: The building has remained a library since then and was renovated in 1960 and the late 1980s. It is a New York City designated landmark and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.fact: An exhibition space designed by Tadao Ando opened at Shikoku Mura in 2002.
facts.quote: An exhibition space designed by Tadao Ando opened in 2002.

facts.fact: Shikoku Mura is an open-air architecture park in Takamatsu with over twenty old buildings from around Shikoku.
facts.quote: Shikoku Mura (四国村) is an open-air architectural park in Takamatsu, Kagawa Prefecture, Japan. It houses over twenty buildings from around Shikoku dating from the Edo period through to the Taishō period, four of which have been designated Important Cultural Properties.

facts.fact: Our Lady of Good Counsel is a Roman Catholic parish church in Dennistoun, Glasgow, and a Category A listed building.
facts.quote: Our Lady of Good Counsel Church is a Roman Catholic Parish Church in the Dennistoun area of Glasgow, Scotland. It is situated on Craigpark. It is a category A listed building.

facts.fact: It was built in 1964–65 to designs by Gillespie, Kidd and Coia.
facts.quote: The church was constructed in 1964-65. The architects were Gillespie, Kidd and Coia.

facts.fact: In 1966 the building won the RIBA bronze regional medal and a Civic Trust Award.
facts.quote: In 1966 they were awarded the bronze regional medal of the RIBA and the Civic Trust Award for this building.

facts.fact: It is one of the firm's geometric churches with sweeping roofs, built with new techniques such as glued laminated timber.
facts.quote: St Mary's, Bo'ness (1962), since demolished; St Joseph's, Faifley, (1964); Our Lady of Good Counsel, Dennistoun, (1965); St Benedict's, Easterhouse, (1965); and St. Paul's, Glenrothes, (1956) were all geometric buildings with sweeping roofs, using new construction techniques, such as glued laminated timber.

facts.fact: Richard Riemerschmid built the Carl villa in Feldafing in 1910–12 for the publisher Hans Carl.
facts.quote: 1910–12: Carl villa, for the publisher Hans Carl, Höhenbergstraße 35, Feldafing

facts.fact: Guildford Cathedral, the Anglican cathedral of Guildford, was designed by Edward Maufe and built between 1936 and 1961.
facts.quote: Designed by Edward Maufe and built between 1936 and 1961, it is the seat of the Bishop of Guildford.

facts.fact: Maufe won the 1932 competition, first among 183 entries, with a Gothic design in concrete faced in brick.
facts.quote: In 1932, Maufe won a competition to design the Guildford Cathedral, coming first among 183 entries with a Gothic design in concrete faced in brick.

facts.fact: Maufe aimed for a design of his own time in the line of the great English cathedrals, relying on proportion, mass, volume and line rather than ornament.
facts.quote: Writing in 1932, Maufe said: "The ideal has been to produce a design, definitely of our own time, yet in the line of the great English Cathedrals; to build anew on tradition, to rely on proportion, mass, volume and line rather than on elaboration and ornament."

facts.fact: Inspired by Albi Cathedral, Maufe used narrow 'passage aisles' to give a broad, open nave without flying buttresses.
facts.quote: He aimed to create a broad and uninterrupted nave space by the use of narrow "passage aisles", which as at Albi, removed the need for flying buttresses.

facts.fact: When stone proved too costly, Maufe brought back a medieval brick from Albi for Guildford brickmakers to copy.
facts.quote: When it became apparent that economy would preclude the use of stone, Maufe brought a medieval brick back from Albi, which was copied by the Guildford brick makers for use in the new building.

facts.fact: The cathedral stands on Stag Hill, and its solid red brick outline can be seen for miles.
facts.quote: Where to put the cathedral for the new diocese of Guildford was a vexing question until Richard, Lord Onslow donated 6 acres (2.4 ha) atop Stag Hill — so named because the Kings of England used to hunt there. Its solid red brick outline is visible for miles around.

facts.fact: Inside, pale Somerset limestone pillars and white Italian marble floors make it seem filled with light; the tower is 160 ft high.
facts.quote: The tower is 160 feet (49 m) high, and contains twelve bells. At the top of the tower stands a 15-foot (4.6 m) gilded angel, which turns in the wind. Inside, the cathedral appears to be filled with light, with pale Somerset limestone pillars and white Italian marble floors.

facts.fact: It was the last Church of England cathedral consecrated on a new site; it was listed Grade II* in 1981.
facts.quote: The cathedral was listed as Grade II* by Historic England in 1981. It was the last Church of England cathedral to be consecrated on a new site, and one of only three to be built in the 20th century, the others being Liverpool and Coventry Cathedral.

facts.fact: In 1943 Max Frisch was chosen from 65 applicants to design the Letzigraben pool in Zürich's Albisrieden district, now renamed Max-Frisch-Bad.
facts.quote: In 1943 Frisch was selected from among 65 applicants to design the new Letzigraben (subsequently renamed Max-Frisch-Bad) swimming pool in the Zurich district of Albisrieden.

facts.fact: The commission let Frisch open his own architecture studio.
facts.quote: Because of this substantial commission he was able to open his own architecture studio, with a couple of employees.

facts.fact: Wartime material shortages delayed construction until 1947, and the public pool opened in 1949.
facts.quote: Wartime materials shortages meant that construction had to be deferred until 1947, but the public swimming pool was opened in 1949.

facts.fact: The landscape architect Gustav Ammann worked with Frisch on the open-air pool in 1947–1949.
facts.quote: Collaborating with architect Max Frisch, he worked on the Freibad Letzigraben open-air swimming pool in Zürich (1947–1949).

facts.fact: The pool is now a protected monument and was restored to its original condition in 2006–2007.
facts.quote: It is now protected under historic monument legislation. From 2006 to 2007, it underwent an extensive renovation which returned it to its original condition.

facts.fact: Skogskapellet, the Woodland Chapel, was designed in 1920 by Gunnar Asplund in Stockholm's Woodland Cemetery.
facts.quote: The project was inspired by the Skogskapellet (English: Woodland Chapel), designed in 1920 by the architect Erik Gunnar Asplund in the Skogskyrkogården (English: Woodland Cemetery) in Stockholm, Sweden.

facts.fact: The Woodland Cemetery opened in 1920 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1994); its design by Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz runs from Nordic Classicism to mature functionalism.
facts.quote: It was inaugurated in 1920 and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994. Its design, by Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz, reflects the development of architecture from Nordic Classicism to mature functionalism.

facts.fact: Asplund and Lewerentz's entry 'Tallum' won the 1915 competition, and work began in 1917 on old gravel pits overgrown with pines.
facts.quote: The entry called "Tallum" by the young architects Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz was selected. After changes made to the design on the recommendations of the competition jury, work began in 1917 on land that had been old gravel quarries that were overgrown with pine trees, and the first phase was completed three years later.

facts.fact: The architects designed the whole cemetery, from the landscape to the smallest lamp, with sculptures by Carl Milles.
facts.quote: The architects designed the entire complex, from the landscape to the smallest lamp, though there are also integrated sculptures by Carl Milles.

facts.fact: In 2018 the Holy See's Vatican Chapels at the Venice Architecture Biennale reimagined Asplund's 1920 Forest Chapel.
facts.quote: Led by directors Francesco Dal Co and Micol Forti, the project team included eleven international architects, who reimagined Gunnar Asplund's 1920 Forest Chapel in Stockholm's cemetery within the contemporary socio-cultural context.

facts.fact: Asplund's drawings for the chapel, in graphite, coloured pencil and ink, date from 1918 to 1921.
facts.quote: The materials used include graphite, coloured pencils, pen and black ink and were created between 1918 and 1921.

facts.fact: Nymble, the KTH student union building in Stockholm, was designed by Uno Åhrén and Sven Markelius in 1928, opened in 1930, is one of the first modernist buildings in Sweden and is listed.
facts.quote: The union building Nymble was designed  by leading Swedish modernists Uno Åhrén and Sven Markelius in 1928 and inaugurated in 1930; it is significant as one of the first examples of modernist architecture in Sweden and has status as a listed building.

facts.fact: The Finnish pavilion in the Giardini was designed by Alvar and Elissa Aalto and built in 1955–1956.
facts.quote: The pavilion, designed by Alvar Aalto and Elissa Aalto, was built between 1955 and 1956.

facts.fact: It was meant as a temporary space for Finland's show at the 28th Biennale but is still in use; it is the only Aalto building in Italy finished in his lifetime.
facts.quote: It was originally designed as a temporary space for the Finnish national exhibition at the 28th Venice Biennale, but it remains in use today. It is the only Alvar Aalto building in Italy that was completed during Aalto's lifetime.

facts.fact: It is a prefabricated structure with a trapezoidal plan.
facts.quote: The Giardini now hosts 30 pavilions of foreign countries, some of them designed by architects such as Josef Hoffmann's Austria Pavilion, Gerrit Thomas Rietveld's Dutch pavilion or the Finnish pavilion, a pre-fabricated structure with a trapezoidal plan designed by Alvar Aalto.

facts.fact: It is built mainly of wood, a hard material in humid, flood-prone Venice, and is fully coated and painted against sun and water.
facts.quote: The building is constructed primarily of wood, a challenging material for the humid and flood‑prone Venice. The pavilion is fully coated and painted, providing a layer of protection from sunlight and water.

facts.fact: After the shared Nordic pavilion opened in 1962 it was lent to other countries; Finland has used it again since 2007.
facts.quote: After the shared Nordic pavilion was completed in 1962, the building was lent to other countries, including Italy, Argentina, Portugal, and Iceland. It has been used again by the Finnish national exhibition since 2007.

facts.fact: Fredrik Fogh restored it in 1976–1982, with a further restoration in 1993.
facts.quote: The building was restored by Fredrik Fogh between 1976 and 1982, with a further restoration taking place in 1993.

facts.fact: Finland's 2025 Architecture Biennale exhibition used the pavilion itself to show architecture as a shared task of stewardship.
facts.quote: The exhibition at the pavilion for the 19th Venice Biennale of Architecture in 2025 was titled The Pavilion – Architecture of Stewardship and used the pavilion itself as an example of architecture as a collaborative task: architects, engineers, construction workers, maintenance staff, cleaners, and other roles all play a part in the creation and upkeep of any building over its lifetime.

facts.fact: Renaat Braem designed the house, 'Huis Braem-Severin', in 1950 at Menegemlei 23 in Deurne, Antwerp; his wife Elza Severin helped with the interior.
facts.quote: In 1950 Renaat Bream designed their house called "Huis Braem-Severin". Elza Severin helped with the interior design. It is located in Deurne, Antwerp, Menegemlei 23.

facts.fact: Braem's works list dates his private house at Menegemlei 23 to 1955.
facts.quote: Private house of Renaat Braem (1955), Menegemlei 23, Antwerp

facts.fact: Its exterior and interior are based on the golden ratio, in a modernist style.
facts.quote: The exterior and interior are based on the natural ratio of the golden ratio. The style of the building belongs to the modernist architecture movement.

facts.fact: In 1999 the house and all its contents (archive, library, furniture) were left to the Flemish Community.
facts.quote: His private home, built in 1955, and all its contents (archive, library, furniture) was legated to the Flemish Community in 1999.

facts.fact: The house became a museum, the second of its kind in Belgium after the Horta Museum in Brussels.
facts.quote: His house was transformed into a museum, the second of its kind in Belgium after the Horta Museum in Brussels.

facts.fact: Albert Einstein's summer house in Caputh was built in 1929 to a design by Konrad Wachsmann.
facts.quote: Summer house of Albert Einstein in Caputh, built in 1929 and designed by Konrad Wachsmann.

facts.fact: The wooden house is Einstein's only surviving residence in Germany.
facts.quote: The wooden house, built in 1929 by the architect Konrad Wachsmann, is Einstein's only preserved residence in Germany.

facts.fact: Einstein, a keen sailor on the lake, could use the retreat only until the Nazi takeover in 1933.
facts.quote: Einstein, though a non swimmer, was a passionate recreational sailor on the lake, but was only able to use his retreat until the Nazi takeover in 1933.

facts.fact: After reunification and restitution it became the property of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and the Einstein Forum uses it for conferences and lectures.
facts.quote: After German reunification and the restitution to the Einstein family, the house is now a property of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. The Einstein Forum, directed since 2000 by Susan Neiman, uses Einstein's summerhouse for conferences, workshops, and lectures.

facts.fact: Julio Vilamajó built the house for his family in Montevideo in 1930; it was the first modern house in Uruguay to open as a museum.
facts.quote: The Vilamajó House Museum (Spanish: Museo Casa Vilamajó) is located in the house that the architect Julio Vilamajó built for his family in 1930 in Montevideo, being the first modern dwelling to open its doors as a museum house in Uruguay.

facts.fact: Vilamajó built the house as his own home at a time when he was moving from a historical to a humanist standpoint, seeking to balance logic and rationality.
facts.quote: He built their own home in Montevideo; it is now the Vilamajó House Museum. This was a time of transition when Vilamajó began to move from a historical to a humanist standpoint, seeking to balance logic and rationality in his construction projects.

facts.fact: The house was declared a National Historic Landmark in 1990.
facts.quote: The dwelling itself, a modern and unique piece of work declared a National Historic Landmark in 1990, is the main component and an ideal platform for housing a permanent exhibition on the work of Vilamajó, and for the regular showcasing of temporary exhibitions related not only to architecture and design, but also to related areas.

facts.fact: The museum, an initiative of the University of the Republic's School of Architecture, opened in May 2012.
facts.quote: The Vilamajó House Museum is the materialization of an initiative of the School of Architecture at the University of the Republic which, in agreement with the Ministry of Education and Culture, owner of the property, opened its doors to the public in May 2012.

facts.fact: The interiors were carefully restored with the original furniture, artwork and belongings, and the gardens replanted with their original species.
facts.quote: The building and its facilities have been fully recovered and thanks to the careful restoration of its interiors, including the original furniture, artwork and personal belongings, the former attractions of the professor's home can now be appreciated. Its gardens have also been remodeled, reincorporating plant species which were initially included there.
